title: 道德經 第十九章
source: Laozi 老子, 道德經 (Daodejing), chapter 19, in the Wang Bi 王弼 recension (華亭張氏原本, 晉 王弼注), as transcribed at Chinese Wikisource; verified character-for-character against the printed public-domain edition of Paul Carus, Lao-Tze's Tao-Teh-King: Chinese-English (Chicago: Open Court, 1898), p. 62. All punctuation is editorial — the original has none — and the division into 81 chapters is traditional. Sense-units follow Wang Bi's own commentary lemmata. Translations are made fresh from the Chinese. Pronunciation convention: modern Mandarin, given in Hanyu Pinyin — an admitted anachronism, and the living convention for reading these texts. Where an Old Chinese rhyme is invisible in Mandarin, a note says so. Prepared audio is synthesized speech in that same convention (cmn-CN-Chirp3-HD-Achernar).
about: Chapter 19 of the Daodejing. Its traditional title is 還淳 (Back to the Unadulterated). The chapter titles are not part of the text and are not Wang Bi's: they come from the Heshanggong 河上公 recension and are carried here only as navigation labels, so a chapter can be found by something other than its number. The received text is Wang Bi's (3rd c. AD); the manuscripts found at Mawangdui (1973) and Guodian (1993) are older and differ in places, and the notes flag those differences where they matter. Classical Chinese has no inflection, no obligatory subject, and no fixed parts of speech — the notes show how the line produces its meaning. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

sentences.t:
絕聖棄智，
民利百倍；
絕仁棄義，
民復孝慈；
絕巧棄利，
盜賊無有。
此三者以為文不足，
故令有所屬﹕
見素抱樸，
少私寡欲。

sentences.i: Have done with sagehood, throw away cleverness, and the people profit a hundredfold; have done with humaneness, throw away rightness, and the people come back to devotion between parent and child; have done with contrivance, throw away gain, and there will be no robbers or brigands. As a form of words these three are not enough, so give men something to hold to: show the undyed silk, keep hold of the uncarved block, be sparing of self and make your wants few.
sentences.n: The whole chapter is one sense-unit — Wang Bi lets it run to the end before he comments. Three commands, each four characters, each followed by its result, and not one of them marked as a conditional: the 'and then' is yours to supply, exactly as in chapter 18. Watch the parts of speech slide: 利 'benefit' becomes the verb 'profit', 少 'few' becomes 'make few', 見 is read xiàn 'show' rather than jiàn 'see'. That last one is a real decision — some read 見素 as 'look upon plainness', but 抱樸 beside it is a thing done with the hands, so we take 見 as the causative to match. 樸, the uncarved block, is the one place where we keep the standard English rendering: it is exact, and nothing better exists. 文 is the other decision: the character is 'pattern, writing', and it can mean outward show or it can mean the wording itself. Wang Bi takes the second — the three commands, baldly stated, do not say enough on their own, which is why the text goes on to supply something positive to hold to; and he reads 此三者 as the three pairs renounced, not the three orders. The big manuscript news is here: the Guodian bamboo slips (c. 300 BC), the oldest witness we have, do not attack 聖 and 仁義 by name at all. Where the received text reads 絕聖棄智 and 絕仁棄義, the slips have something closer to 'cut off knowing, throw away disputation' and 'cut off artifice, throw away scheming' — the target is cleverness and pretence, not the Confucian virtues. If that is the older text, the sharpest anti-Confucian passage in the book was sharpened later. The reading of the slips is itself argued over, so hold it loosely. Sound: 足, 屬, 樸 and 欲 all belong to one Old Chinese rhyme group, which is why these last lines come as a run; Mandarin keeps a shadow of it in zú, shǔ and pǔ and loses it in yù.
